content_topics: Classification of plants (flowering and non-flowering plants).
Parts and functions of flowers.
learning_experiences: use print and non-print materials to search for images of flowering and non-flowering plants and share,
take a walk in their locality to observe, identify and categorise plants into flowering and non-flowering,
draw a flower and label parts,
discuss functions of parts of a flower and share with peers,
discuss the importance of flowers in nature with peers,
use digital applications to draw, paint and label flowers.
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and imagination: The learner reflects and draw accurate images as they draw a flower and label parts.
Digital literacy: The learner acquire digital manipulative skills as they use digital applications to draw, paint and label flowers.
sub_strands.values: Unity: The learner appreciates sharing of the available resources amicably as they draw a flower and label parts.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental Conservation: The learner conserves the environment by not destroying plants as they observing, identifying and categorising plants into flowering and non-flowering in their natural habitat.
sub_strands.links: Creative Arts: The use of digital applications to draw, paint and label flowers is linked to drawing and painting in Creative Arts.
sub_strands.design_notes: Learners are guided on precautions to take when handling plants as they study flowering and non-flowering plants.

outcomes.text: classify plants into flowering and non-flowering
describe functions of parts of a flower
outline the importance of flowers in nature
appreciate the importance of flowers in nature

skills.name: Classify plants as flowering or non-flowering
skills.mastery: Given a plant the child knows in Kenya (maize, beans, kale, mango, tomato, banana, grass, cypress, pine, fern, moss), says whether it is a flowering or a non-flowering plant and gives the reason: flowering plants make flowers, fruits and seeds; non-flowering plants (ferns, mosses, cypress and pine) make spores or cones instead. The child does not judge by whether the plant is flowering this week or by whether the flower is showy. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: sort a named plant into flowering or non-flowering
pick the list that holds only flowering plants
read a table of plant observations and decide
say why a plant with no flower this week is still flowering

prerequisites.reason: Grade 4 introduced plants as living things.
Knowing the external parts of a plant helps the child look for flowers.

skills.name: Name the main parts of a flower
skills.mastery: Given a labelled or described flower, the child names the petals (the bright or coloured parts), the sepals (the small green parts below the petals that covered the bud), the stamens (each with an anther on a thin stalk), and the pistil (stigma at the top, style, and ovary at the base). The child can tell the stamens from the pistil. Proposed: anther, filament, stigma, style and ovary are used as extra names; a teacher confirms how far Grade 5 goes. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the part from where it is and what it looks like
match a part to its position in a flower described in words
which part is not in this flower description
complete a short label list

prerequisites.reason: External parts of a plant; the flower is one of them.

skills.name: Describe the functions of the parts of a flower
skills.mastery: The child says what each part does: petals attract insects, birds and bees; sepals protect the flower while it is still a bud; the anther makes pollen; the stigma catches pollen; the ovary holds the ovules that become seeds. Given a job, the child names the part; given a part, the child gives its job. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: match a part to its job
which part does this job
cause and effect: what is lost if a part is removed
short typed answer: the part that makes pollen

prerequisites.reason: The child must know the part before learning its job.

skills.name: Explain how a flower becomes a fruit with seeds
skills.mastery: The child puts the steps in order: insects, wind or birds carry pollen from the anther to the stigma (pollination); after that the ovules grow into seeds and the ovary grows into the fruit. The child knows that fruits such as tomatoes, mangoes and pumpkins come from flowers, and that with no pollen arriving a flower usually makes no fruit. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: put the steps in order
cause and effect: what happens if bees cannot reach the flowers
which part becomes the fruit
tell pollination apart from carrying seeds away

prerequisites.reason: Pollen, stigma and ovary jobs are needed to follow the steps.

skills.name: Outline the importance of flowers in nature
skills.mastery: The child gives at least three importances of flowers and links each to a real example: flowers become fruits and seeds (food for people and animals, new plants); flowers feed bees and other insects with nectar and pollen (and bees give honey); flowers are sold for income (cut flowers from Naivasha), used for decoration, and some give medicine or tea. The child does not say flowers are only for decoration. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the importance that is true
which statement is not an importance of flowers
cause and effect: what is lost if there were no flowers
sort uses into food, income, home and nature

prerequisites.reason: Fruits and seeds from flowers are the central importance.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a plant with no big, bright flowers (maize, grass, kale, mango) does not flower.

example.question: Is a maize plant a flowering plant or a non-flowering plant?
example.wrong_answer: Non-flowering plant
example.correct_answer: Flowering plant

misconceptions.cause: The child counts only showy petals as flowers. The flowers of maize (the tassel and the silk), grasses and many trees are small and green or yellow.
misconceptions.reveals: Use crops and grasses, never roses or hibiscus, and offer the answer "non-flowering".
misconceptions.help: Look closely at a maize tassel and a young cob with the class and call both flowers. Anything that makes seeds inside a fruit or grain belongs to the flowering plants.
misconceptions.feedback: Many flowers are small and not bright. Maize has flowers too: the tassel at the top and the silk on the cob. A plant that makes seeds inside fruits or grains is a flowering plant.
misconceptions.source: Plant-concept research reports that children restrict 'flower' to showy flowers (Bell and Barker 1982; Tunnicliffe and Reiss 1999). Cited from memory: verify the references.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every tree is a flowering plant, including cypress and pine, which make cones.

example.question: Is a cypress tree a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
example.wrong_answer: Flowering plant
example.correct_answer: Non-flowering plant

misconceptions.cause: The child sorts by size or by being a plant with seeds, and has not met cones as a different way of making seeds.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer cypress or pine next to mango and ask for flowering or non-flowering.
misconceptions.help: Show a cypress cone. Cones hold seeds but they are not flowers and there is no fruit. Compare with a mango flower and fruit.
misconceptions.feedback: Cypress and pine are trees, but they make cones, not flowers and fruits. That makes them non-flowering plants.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every plant has flowers, so ferns and mosses must flower too.

example.question: Does a fern make flowers?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, but very small ones
example.correct_answer: No

misconceptions.cause: The child assumes all green plants flower, because the plants at home and at school all do.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask about ferns or mosses and offer "yes, hidden flowers".
misconceptions.help: Look at the underside of a fern frond for the spore cases, and at moss capsules. These plants never make flowers.
misconceptions.feedback: Ferns and mosses never make flowers. They make tiny spores instead. They are non-flowering plants.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Decides by what the plant looks like today: a bean or kale plant with no flower this week is "non-flowering".

example.question: A kale plant in a shamba has no flowers this week. Is kale a non-flowering plant?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has no flowers now
example.correct_answer: No, kale makes flowers when it is left to grow

misconceptions.cause: The child classifies by the moment of looking, not by what the plant can do over its whole life.
misconceptions.reveals: Describe a flowering plant that has not flowered yet, such as a bean seedling or kale cut every week.
misconceptions.help: Follow one bean plant through weeks: seedling, flower, pod. A plant is flowering if it makes flowers at some time in its life.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at the whole life of the plant. Kale and beans make flowers when they are old enough, even if you do not see any today. They are flowering plants.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge: children judge living-thing and plant status by what is visible at the time. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up petals and sepals, calling the small green parts below the flower the petals.

example.question: Which part is the small green leaf-like part at the base of a flower?
example.wrong_answer: Petal
example.correct_answer: Sepal

misconceptions.cause: The child names the part by the word they know best (petal) and has not looked at the green ring under the coloured petals.
misconceptions.reveals: Describe the green part by position and colour and offer petal as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Take a bean or hibiscus flower apart. Petals are coloured and on the inside. Sepals are green and underneath, and they covered the bud.
misconceptions.feedback: Petals are the coloured parts. The green parts at the bottom that covered the flower when it was a bud are the sepals.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Swaps the stamen and the pistil.

example.question: Which part of a flower is the stamen?
example.wrong_answer: The part in the middle with the ovary at its base
example.correct_answer: The part with a thin stalk and a small pollen-holding top

misconceptions.cause: The words sound alike and both stand in the middle of the flower.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the part with pollen, and offer the pistil.
misconceptions.help: Say the rhyme: STamen has the pollen (Sticks up with an anther), PIStil has the Pip (seed) place. Draw both from a real flower.
misconceptions.feedback: The stamens are the thin stalks that carry the pollen on top. The pistil is the part in the middle that has the ovary at its base.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the stigma is the top of the stamen, or that the anther is part of the pistil.

example.question: Which part of a flower is sticky and catches pollen?
example.wrong_answer: Anther
example.correct_answer: Stigma

misconceptions.cause: The child knows both are small knobs at the top of a thin part and mixes them up.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask which part holds pollen and which part catches pollen, with both names as options.
misconceptions.help: Pollen is made on the anther (A for "at the stamen") and lands on the sticky stigma (S for "sticky").
misconceptions.feedback: The anther is the top of the stamen and holds the pollen. The stigma is the sticky top of the pistil, where pollen lands.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the sepals the job of attracting insects and the petals the job of protecting the bud.

example.question: Which part of a flower protects the bud before it opens?
example.wrong_answer: Petals
example.correct_answer: Sepals

misconceptions.cause: The child has swapped the two names or has assumed the bigger, brighter part does the protecting.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the protecting part and offer petals first.
misconceptions.help: Show a bud: the green sepals wrap it. Then show an open flower: the bright petals are the sign for insects.
misconceptions.feedback: Sepals are the tough green parts that wrap the bud. Petals are bright to attract insects and birds.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks pollen is a seed, or that the stamen makes the seeds.

example.question: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
example.wrong_answer: Ovary
example.correct_answer: Anther

misconceptions.cause: The child links a flower with seeds and has not separated pollen (made on the anther) from seeds (made in the ovary after pollen arrives).
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what the stamen makes and offer "seeds".
misconceptions.help: Rub an anther on paper to see the yellow pollen. Then cut open a young bean pod: the seeds grow in the ovary. They are different things.
misconceptions.feedback: Pollen is a fine dust made on the anther. Seeds grow later inside the ovary. Pollen is not a seed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the ovary the job of making pollen, or gives the anther the job of holding the seeds.

example.question: Which part of a flower holds the ovules that later become seeds?
example.wrong_answer: Anther
example.correct_answer: Ovary

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the flower makes both pollen and seeds but has not tied each to its own part.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer the anther as the part that holds ovules.
misconceptions.help: Make a two-column chart: anther - makes pollen; ovary - holds ovules, later the seeds.
misconceptions.feedback: The ovary is at the base of the pistil and holds the ovules that become seeds. The anther makes pollen.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks fruits grow straight from the stem or roots, not from the flower.

example.question: From which part of a pumpkin plant does the pumpkin fruit grow?
example.wrong_answer: The root
example.correct_answer: The flower (its ovary)

misconceptions.cause: The child sees fruit hanging from the plant and has never watched the flower wither and the fruit swell in its place.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask where a fruit comes from and offer root or stem.
misconceptions.help: Watch a tomato or pumpkin flower for two weeks: the petals drop and the base of the flower swells into the fruit.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at what grows where the flower was. The petals fall off and the ovary at the base swells to become the fruit.
misconceptions.source: Children often do not link fruits with flowers (Driver et al. 1994 on plant reproduction). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up pollination (carrying pollen to a stigma) with carrying seeds away to new places.

example.question: A bee moves from one pumpkin flower to another with yellow dust on its legs. What is happening?
example.wrong_answer: Seeds are being carried to a new place
example.correct_answer: Pollen is being carried to a stigma

misconceptions.cause: The child knows animals and wind help plants spread and uses one idea for both jobs.
misconceptions.reveals: Describe pollen movement and offer seed dispersal.
misconceptions.help: Two charts: pollination is before the seed (pollen to stigma). Dispersal is after (seed to new ground).
misconceptions.feedback: Pollination is carrying pollen from an anther to a stigma. Carrying seeds away to new places is another job, called seed dispersal.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks flowers make fruits whether or not pollen ever reaches them, so bees and the wind do not matter.

example.question: A farmer sprays a pesticide that kills all the bees near his pumpkin flowers. What is likely to happen to the pumpkins?
example.wrong_answer: They will still grow just as many fruits
example.correct_answer: Fewer fruits will grow

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the plant fills the fruit on its own and does not link pollen arriving with seeds starting to grow.
misconceptions.reveals: Give a scenario with no pollinators and offer "no change".
misconceptions.help: Compare a flower covered with a net bag (no visitors) and an open one over two weeks.
misconceptions.feedback: Many flowers, such as pumpkin and passion fruit, need pollen to be carried to them. With no bees, fewer flowers are pollinated and fewer fruits grow.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks flowers are only for decoration and smell.

example.question: Why are flowers important in nature, apart from looking beautiful?
example.wrong_answer: They are only there to look and smell nice
example.correct_answer: They make fruits and seeds and feed bees and other insects

misconceptions.cause: The child knows flowers from bouquets and gardens and has not thought about what they do for the plant.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the importance of flowers and offer "to look nice" as an answer.
misconceptions.help: List everything on the lunch plate that began as a flower: maize, beans, mango, tomato.
misconceptions.feedback: Flowers are much more than decoration. They make the fruits and seeds we eat, they feed bees, and they bring in money for farmers.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks insects on flowers harm the plant and should be killed.

example.question: Bees visit the flowers on Wanjiru's bean plants. What should she think about the bees?
example.wrong_answer: They help the plant make seeds, so she should leave them
example.correct_answer: They are harming the plant, so she should kill them

misconceptions.cause: The child knows some insects eat crops and lumps all insects together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "kill the insects" as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Show a bee carrying pollen. Separate insects that eat leaves from those that carry pollen.
misconceptions.feedback: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, so the plant can make seeds. They help, and they also give us honey.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not link everyday foods (mango, beans, tomato, maize grain) with flowers.

example.question: Which food came from a flower?
example.wrong_answer: Cassava roots
example.correct_answer: Mangoes

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of flowers as separate from food plants.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask which food came from a flower and offer a root.
misconceptions.help: Trace a mango back to the mango flower in a season of the year.
misconceptions.feedback: Fruits and grains grow from flowers. Mangoes, beans, tomatoes and maize all started as flowers.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome d ("appreciate the importance of flowers in nature") is attitudinal: no question family; observe it in a nature walk or a flower portfolio. Outcomes a to c are tested by questions. Drawing and labelling a flower is a practical.

Groups of vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles, fish and amphibians; structural features only)
learning_experiences: search for information from print and non-print material on the general characteristics of vertebrates and share with peers,
explore the school compound and adjacent environment to observe and identify characteristics of vertebrates,
discuss with peers the characteristics of different groups of vertebrates, study their main characteristics.
key_inquiry_questions: What are the key features of vertebrates?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and collaboration: The learner acquires speaking and listening skills as they contribute in the discussions on main characteristics of vertebrates.
Creativity and Imagination: The learner acquires manipulative skills as they skilfully designs and develops a portfolio on vertebrates.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: The learner observes safety precautions when handling different animals.
sub_strands.pcis: Safety and security: The learner observes necessary precautions while handling animals.
sub_strands.links:
Agriculture and Nutrition: The learner links information on characteristics of animals as living things is linked to the study of livestock in Agriculture.

outcomes.text: describe general characteristics of vertebrates
classify vertebrates into their main groups
appreciate the importance of vertebrates in the environment

skills.name: Describe the general characteristics of vertebrates
skills.mastery: The child says that vertebrates are animals with a backbone and an inside skeleton, and tells vertebrates from invertebrates in the environment (cow, goat, fish, snake, frog, hen are vertebrates; butterfly, termite, earthworm, crab, snail are invertebrates). The child does not decide by size, legs or a hard outside. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the animal that is a vertebrate
why is a snake a vertebrate
sort animals into vertebrates and invertebrates
say what all vertebrates have in common

prerequisites.reason: Grade 4 distinguished vertebrates from invertebrates.
Characteristics of animals as living things.

skills.name: Classify vertebrates into mammals, birds, reptiles, fish and amphibians
skills.mastery: Given a vertebrate from Kenya (cow, goat, lion, bat, dolphin, hen, flamingo, ostrich, tilapia, shark, crocodile, snake, chameleon, tortoise, frog), the child names its group using its body features, not where it lives or whether it flies. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which group does this animal belong to
pick the list that holds only one group
odd one out in a list of animals
read a table of features and name the group

prerequisites.reason: The child must first know the animal is a vertebrate.

skills.name: Match body features to the groups of vertebrates
skills.mastery: The child matches features to groups: mammals have hair or fur and feed young on milk; birds have feathers, wings and lay hard-shelled eggs; reptiles have dry scales and lay eggs on land; fish have wet scales, fins and gills; amphibians have moist smooth skin and live part of life in water and part on land. Structural features only, as the design says. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which feature belongs to this group
which feature is found in all birds and no other group
table of features: name the group
which animal has this set of features

prerequisites.reason: Naming the groups and their features support each other.
Features are of vertebrates.

misconceptions.error: Thinks big animals are vertebrates and small animals are not (or the other way round).

example.question: Is a small mouse a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: Invertebrate, because it is small
example.correct_answer: Vertebrate, because it has a backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child uses size, which is easy to see, in place of the backbone, which is hidden.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a very small vertebrate (mouse, gecko) and a big invertebrate (crab, octopus).
misconceptions.help: Feel your own backbone, then compare with the thin skeleton of a small fish.
misconceptions.feedback: Size does not matter. A mouse is small but it has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge: children classify animals by obvious features such as size. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an animal with no legs (snake, fish) cannot be a vertebrate.

example.question: A snake has no legs. Is a snake a vertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: No, because it has no legs
example.correct_answer: Yes, because it has a backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child links "animal with bones" with legs to stand on.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a snake or a fish and offer legs as the reason.
misconceptions.help: Look at a snake skeleton picture: a long backbone with many bones.
misconceptions.feedback: Legs are not needed. A snake has a long backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a hard shell or hard outside (crab, beetle, snail) means the animal has a backbone.

example.question: A crab has a hard shell. Is a crab a vertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because its shell is hard like a bone
example.correct_answer: No, because it has no backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen hard parts on the animal and takes them for bones.
misconceptions.reveals: Use crab, beetle or snail with "hard shell" as the offered reason.
misconceptions.help: Compare the inside skeleton of a fish with the outside shell of a crab.
misconceptions.feedback: A crab has a hard shell on the outside, but no backbone inside. It is an invertebrate.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a bat is a bird because it flies.

example.question: To which group does a bat belong?
example.wrong_answer: Birds
example.correct_answer: Mammals

misconceptions.cause: The child groups by how the animal moves, not by body covering and how the young are fed.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer the bat with birds in the options.
misconceptions.help: A bat has fur and feeds its young on milk. No feathers. Birds have feathers and lay eggs.
misconceptions.feedback: Flying does not make a bird. A bat has fur and feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal.
misconceptions.source: Children group animals by where they live or how they move (Braund 1991; Kattmann 2001). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any animal that lives in water is a fish (dolphin, crocodile, hippo, frog).

example.question: To which group does a dolphin belong?
example.wrong_answer: Fish
example.correct_answer: Mammals

misconceptions.cause: The child groups by habitat, not by body features.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer dolphin or crocodile with fish in the options.
misconceptions.help: Fish have gills and scales. A dolphin breathes air with lungs and feeds its young on milk.
misconceptions.feedback: Living in water does not make a fish. A dolphin breathes air and feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal.
misconceptions.source: Braund 1991; Kattmann 2001: habitat-based grouping. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up reptiles and amphibians (thinking chameleons and lizards are amphibians, or frogs are reptiles).

example.question: To which group does a chameleon belong?
example.wrong_answer: Amphibians
example.correct_answer: Reptiles

misconceptions.cause: The child knows both groups are cold to the touch and lay eggs and has not looked at the skin.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer chameleon or frog with the other group.
misconceptions.help: Reptiles have dry scales and lay eggs on land. Amphibians have moist skin and start life in water.
misconceptions.feedback: A chameleon has dry scales and lays its eggs on land. That makes it a reptile.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a bird that cannot fly (an ostrich) is not a bird.

example.question: To which group does an ostrich belong?
example.wrong_answer: Mammals, because it cannot fly
example.correct_answer: Birds

misconceptions.cause: The child uses flying to define a bird, not feathers and eggs with hard shells.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer ostrich and "cannot fly".
misconceptions.help: List what an ostrich has: feathers, wings, a beak, hard-shelled eggs.
misconceptions.feedback: An ostrich cannot fly, but it has feathers, wings and a beak, and it lays eggs. It is a bird.
misconceptions.source: Braund 1991: a bird must fly. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any animal that lays eggs is a bird.

example.question: A crocodile lays eggs. Is it a bird?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because birds lay eggs
example.correct_answer: No, it is a reptile

misconceptions.cause: The child has learned that birds lay eggs and does not know that other groups do too.
misconceptions.reveals: Use crocodile, tortoise or tilapia with the reason "lays eggs".
misconceptions.help: Make a chart of which groups lay eggs: birds, reptiles, fish, amphibians.
misconceptions.feedback: Birds lay eggs, but so do reptiles, fish and amphibians. A crocodile has dry scales, so it is a reptile.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only fish have scales, so snakes and crocodiles do not.

example.question: Which group of vertebrates has dry scales and lays eggs on land?
example.wrong_answer: Fish
example.correct_answer: Reptiles

misconceptions.cause: The child links scales with fish because fish scales are the ones seen at the market.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the group with dry scales and offer fish.
misconceptions.help: Look at a snake skin or a chameleon and feel the dry scales. Compare with wet fish scales.
misconceptions.feedback: Fish have wet scales and live in water. Reptiles such as snakes and crocodiles have dry scales and lay their eggs on land.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any animal with wings is a bird.

example.question: Which feature do all birds have, and no other group of vertebrates?
example.wrong_answer: Wings
example.correct_answer: Feathers

misconceptions.cause: The child uses wings, the most noticeable feature, and forgets that bats and insects have wings too.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the feature found only in birds and offer wings.
misconceptions.help: List flying animals: a bat has wings but fur; a butterfly has wings but no backbone. Only birds have feathers.
misconceptions.feedback: Bats and insects have wings, but only birds have feathers. Feathers are found in birds and no other group.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks amphibians live only in water, or that the word means "lives in water".

example.question: What does it mean when we say a frog is an amphibian?
example.wrong_answer: It lives only in water
example.correct_answer: It spends part of its life in water and part on land

misconceptions.cause: The child connects frogs with ponds and does not know the young live in water and adults can live on land.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask the meaning of amphibian and offer "lives only in water".
misconceptions.help: Follow the life of a frog: eggs and tadpole in water, adult hops on land.
misconceptions.feedback: Amphibians live part of their life in water and part on land. Tadpoles live in water; adult frogs can live on land.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome c ("appreciate the importance of vertebrates in the environment") is attitudinal: no question family; observe it in the portfolio or a school-compound observation. Safety with animals is taught, not tested by a typed question.

Symptoms and prevention of common conditions and diseases of the breathing system (common colds, coughs, COVID-19, allergy and asthma).
learning_experiences: use print and non-print material to identify the human breathing system,
draw the human breathing system and label the main parts,
use print or non-print media to search for information on the functions of main parts of the human breathing system and share with peers,
discuss symptoms and prevention of common conditions and diseases that affect the human breathing system and share,
use simulation or digital images to illustrate major parts of the human breathing system.

What enhances a healthy breathing system?

outcomes.text: identify the main parts of the human breathing system
describe the functions of parts of the human breathing system
coutline the symptoms and prevention measures for common conditions and diseases of the breathing system
appreciate the need for maintaining a healthy breathing system

skills.name: Identify the main parts of the breathing system
skills.mastery: The child names the nose, the windpipe (trachea), the lungs and the diaphragm, says where each is (nose on the face, trachea in the neck and chest, lungs in the upper chest inside the ribs, diaphragm under the lungs), and does not mix the windpipe with the food pipe. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the part from where it is
which part is under the lungs
which part is not part of the breathing system
put the parts in the order air reaches them

prerequisites.reason: Knowing the digestive parts helps the child keep the two pipes apart.

skills.name: Describe the functions of the parts of the breathing system
skills.mastery: The child says what each part does: the nose has hairs and mucus that trap dust and germs, and warms the air; the trachea carries air to the lungs; the lungs take oxygen from the air into the blood and let carbon dioxide out; the diaphragm moves to help the lungs fill and empty. The child knows that air does not go to the stomach, and that breathed-out air still has oxygen in it. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: match the part to its job
cause and effect: what the nose hairs do
what happens in the lungs
which statement about breathing is true

prerequisites.reason: The child names the parts before giving their jobs.

skills.name: Explain what happens in the body when we breathe in and out
skills.mastery: The child says that when we breathe in the diaphragm moves down and the ribs move up and out, the space in the chest gets bigger and air flows in; when we breathe out the diaphragm relaxes and moves up, the ribs move down and in, and air is pushed out. The child can say why the chest rises, and that air flows in because the space got bigger. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what happens to the chest when we breathe in
put the steps of breathing in in order
cause and effect: what makes the air come in
what you can feel with your hands on your chest

prerequisites.reason: Jobs of diaphragm and lungs are needed first.

skills.name: Recognise the symptoms of common breathing conditions
skills.mastery: The child matches symptoms to conditions: sneezing, runny nose and sore throat for a common cold; a cough that may bring up phlegm for a cough or chest infection; fever, dry cough and tiredness (and sometimes loss of taste) for COVID-19; sneezing and itchy eyes after dust or pollen for an allergy; wheezing and short breath for asthma. The child knows asthma and allergy do not spread from one person to another. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: match a symptom to a condition
which condition can spread from person to person
read a short story of a child and name the likely condition
which condition cannot be caught from another person

prerequisites.reason: Symptoms are easier to place if the child knows the parts.

skills.name: Outline how to prevent common breathing conditions
skills.mastery: The child gives sensible ways to prevent breathing illness: cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, wash hands often, keep away from people who are sick, wear a mask in crowded or sick places when asked, keep rooms ventilated, keep dust and smoke away (cook outdoors or with a chimney), and avoid what triggers an allergy or asthma. The child knows a cold comes from a virus, not from cold weather, and that antibiotics do not cure it. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the best way to stop a cold spreading
cause and effect: why smoke in a closed kitchen is a problem
which action does not help
what a child with asthma should avoid

prerequisites.reason: Prevention depends on knowing what causes each condition.

misconceptions.error: Thinks air goes down the same pipe as food, or mixes the windpipe with the food pipe.

example.question: Which pipe carries air from the nose to the lungs?
example.wrong_answer: The food pipe (gullet)
example.correct_answer: The windpipe (trachea)

misconceptions.cause: The child knows there is one pipe down the neck and does not know there are two.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer the food pipe as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Feel the ridged windpipe at the front of the neck. The food pipe is behind it and goes to the stomach.
misconceptions.feedback: There are two pipes in the neck. The windpipe, or trachea, carries air to the lungs. The food pipe carries food to the stomach.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not know where the diaphragm is (puts it in the neck, or thinks it is part of the lungs).

example.question: Which part of the breathing system is the sheet of muscle under the lungs?
example.wrong_answer: The trachea
example.correct_answer: The diaphragm

misconceptions.cause: The word is new and is not seen or felt from outside.
misconceptions.reveals: Describe the diaphragm by position and offer the other names.
misconceptions.help: Draw the body with the diaphragm as a dome under the lungs. Feel your belly rise and fall as you breathe.
misconceptions.feedback: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under the lungs. It is the part that moves when you breathe.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the lungs are low in the belly, or that there is just one.

example.question: Where are the lungs?
example.wrong_answer: In the belly, next to the stomach
example.correct_answer: In the chest, inside the ribs

misconceptions.cause: Children draw the body from outside and place the lungs low or in the middle (Mintzes 1984 reports young children's body-organ drawings).
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the position of the lungs and offer the belly.
misconceptions.help: Put hands on the upper chest and feel the ribs moving. The lungs are behind them.
misconceptions.feedback: There are two lungs, high in the chest and protected by the ribs. The stomach is lower, in the belly.
misconceptions.source: Mintzes (1984), Naive theories in biology: children's concepts of the human body, School Science and Mathematics. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the air we breathe goes to the stomach.

example.question: Where does the air go after the windpipe?
example.wrong_answer: To the stomach
example.correct_answer: To the lungs

misconceptions.cause: The child has not separated the two pipes and the idea that "air goes down" ends in the belly.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask where air goes after the trachea and offer the stomach.
misconceptions.help: Breathe in with the hands on the chest, then on the belly: the chest and the diaphragm move, the stomach does not take in the air.
misconceptions.feedback: Air goes to the lungs, not to the stomach. The stomach is for food. Your belly only moves because the diaphragm moves.
misconceptions.source: Mann and Treagust (1998), pencil-and-paper instrument on breathing, gas exchange and respiration, Australian Science Teachers Journal. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the lungs have muscles and fill and empty themselves like balloons.

example.question: What helps the lungs fill with air when you breathe in?
example.wrong_answer: The lungs pull the air in by themselves
example.correct_answer: The diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs

misconceptions.cause: The child treats the lungs as the only moving part, like a balloon that inflates itself.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what makes air come in and offer the lungs themselves.
misconceptions.help: Use a bottle with a balloon inside and a balloon sheet at the bottom to model the diaphragm.
misconceptions.feedback: The lungs have no muscles. The diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs move, and that makes the lungs fill and empty.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks we breathe in only oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide.

example.question: Which statement about the air we breathe out is true?
example.wrong_answer: It has no oxygen in it at all
example.correct_answer: It still has some oxygen, and more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard "oxygen in, carbon dioxide out" and takes it as the whole story.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what is in breathed-out air and offer "no oxygen".
misconceptions.help: Remind the class that mouth-to-mouth breathing works because breathed-out air has oxygen left.
misconceptions.feedback: Breathed-out air has less oxygen than the air we breathe in, but it still has some. It also has more carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.source: Mann and Treagust (1998). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the nose is only for smelling.

example.question: Besides smelling, what do the hairs and mucus in the nose do?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, the nose is only for smelling
example.correct_answer: They trap dust and germs from the air we breathe in

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the nose as a sense organ and not as a part of the breathing system.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what else the nose does and offer "nothing".
misconceptions.help: Look at a tissue after a dusty day: the dust has been trapped in the nose.
misconceptions.feedback: The nose also cleans and warms the air. The hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and germs before the air reaches the lungs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the chest gets smaller or the ribs move in when we breathe in.

example.question: What happens to the chest when you breathe in?
example.wrong_answer: It gets smaller as the ribs move in
example.correct_answer: It gets bigger as the ribs move up and out

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of "squeezing" the air in, not of making space for it.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what the chest does when breathing in and offer "it gets smaller".
misconceptions.help: Put both hands on the ribs and take a deep breath: feel them move out and up.
misconceptions.feedback: When you breathe in, the ribs move up and out and the diaphragm moves down. The chest gets bigger and air comes in.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the air fills the chest and pushes the ribs out, so the air does the work.

example.question: What is the first thing that happens when you breathe in?
example.wrong_answer: Air rushes in and pushes the chest out
example.correct_answer: The diaphragm and rib muscles move and the chest gets bigger

misconceptions.cause: The child reverses cause and effect: air arrives first, the chest follows.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what comes first and offer "air comes in".
misconceptions.help: Use a bell-jar model: pulling the rubber sheet down makes the balloon fill. The air follows the space.
misconceptions.feedback: The muscles move first. The chest gets bigger, and then air flows in to fill the space. The air does not push the chest out.
misconceptions.source: Mann and Treagust (1998). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks asthma can be caught from another person.

example.question: Can a child catch asthma from a classmate who has it?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it spreads like a cold
example.correct_answer: No, asthma does not spread from person to person

misconceptions.cause: The child treats every illness of the chest or throat as catching.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask whether asthma spreads and offer "yes".
misconceptions.help: Compare asthma (airways narrow, not an infection) with a cold (a virus that spreads).
misconceptions.feedback: Asthma is not an infection. A child with asthma cannot pass it on. Dust, smoke or cold air can start an asthma attack.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sneezing and itchy eyes from dust or pollen are a cold caught from someone.

example.question: Wambui sneezes and has itchy eyes every time she sweeps the dusty classroom. What is the most likely cause?
example.wrong_answer: She has caught a cold from another child
example.correct_answer: She has an allergy to the dust

misconceptions.cause: The child links sneezing with colds only.
misconceptions.reveals: Give the sneezing story with dust and offer "caught a cold".
misconceptions.help: Ask when the sneezing starts and stops: if it begins with dust and ends when the dust is gone, it points to an allergy.
misconceptions.feedback: Sneezing that starts with dust or pollen and stops without it is an allergy, not a cold. An allergy cannot be caught from another person.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks all coughs and colds are the same illness with the same cause.

example.question: Which of these can spread from one person to another?
example.wrong_answer: Asthma
example.correct_answer: A common cold

misconceptions.cause: The child treats every breathing problem as "a cough".
misconceptions.reveals: Ask which can spread and put asthma or allergy next to the cold.
misconceptions.help: List causes: cold and COVID-19 by viruses, asthma and allergy by sensitive airways.
misconceptions.feedback: Colds and COVID-19 are caused by viruses and spread between people. Asthma and allergy do not spread.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a cold is caused by cold weather, rain or a cold drink.

example.question: What causes a common cold?
example.wrong_answer: Cold weather and getting wet in the rain
example.correct_answer: A virus that spreads from one person to another

misconceptions.cause: Colds are more common in the cold season and the child links the two as cause and effect.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask for the cause of a cold and offer cold weather.
misconceptions.help: Show how the cold spreads when someone coughs without covering. Weather can help the virus spread but does not cause it.
misconceptions.feedback: A cold is caused by a virus that spreads from person to person. Cold weather does not cause it.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge (children's ideas about illness and germs). Cited from memory; to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks medicine called antibiotics cures a cold or COVID-19.

example.question: Juma has a cold. What helps him get better?
example.wrong_answer: Taking antibiotics, which kill the cold virus
example.correct_answer: Rest and drinking water; antibiotics do not kill viruses

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard that clinics give medicine for coughs and thinks one medicine fits all illnesses.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what cures a cold and offer antibiotics.
misconceptions.help: Separate viruses (colds, COVID-19) from bacteria (some chest infections). Only a health worker decides on medicine.
misconceptions.feedback: Antibiotics do not kill viruses, and a cold is caused by a virus. Rest and water help. Go to a clinic if the cough is bad or does not go away.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher or health worker before use with children.

misconceptions.error: Thinks washing hands does not matter for illnesses of the breathing system.

example.question: Why does washing hands help to stop a cold spreading?
example.wrong_answer: It does not help, because colds are only in the nose
example.correct_answer: Germs on the hands can reach the nose and mouth

misconceptions.cause: The child connects handwashing with stomach illnesses only.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask why wash hands to stop a cold and offer "it does not help".
misconceptions.help: Show glitter on the hands to see how it reaches the face.
misconceptions.feedback: Hands pick up virus from surfaces and then touch the nose, eyes and mouth. Washing them helps to stop it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks smoke from a cooking fire in a closed room is harmless.

example.question: Why is it better to cook outdoors or in a kitchen with a chimney?
example.wrong_answer: Smoke does not harm the lungs, so it makes no difference
example.correct_answer: Smoke can harm the lungs and make coughing and asthma worse

misconceptions.cause: Smoke from cooking is part of everyday life and the child has never linked it to illness.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask about smoke in the kitchen and offer "no difference".
misconceptions.help: Ask the class how their eyes and chest feel in a smoky kitchen.
misconceptions.feedback: Smoke irritates the nose and lungs. It can bring on coughs and asthma. A chimney or an open door lets it out.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome d ("appreciate the need for maintaining a healthy breathing system") is attitudinal: no question family. The KICD text reads "coutline" in outcome c; it is kept as printed in the outcome and read as "outline". Model-making of the lungs is a practical.

content_topics: Meaning of mixtures
Types of mixtures (heterogeneous and homogeneous).
Examples of mixtures (solid-solid, solid-liquid and liquid -liquid).
Methods of separating heterogeneous mixtures (Winnowing, picking, sieving, using magnet, filtering, decanting, separating funnel).
learning_experiences: brainstorm on the meaning of a mixture, give examples at home and school,
carry out activities to categorise mixtures as homogeneous (uniform) and heterogeneous (non-uniform),
carry out activities to separate heterogeneous mixtures,
carry out activities to demonstrate ways of separating mixtures in day-to-day life.
key_inquiry_questions: What are the applications of mixture separation in day- to-day life?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Critical thinking and imagination: The learner acquires reflects on the best ways of separating different mixtures as they carry out activities to demonstrate ways of separating mixtures.
Learning to learn: The learner learns new methods separating mixtures through their own experiences as they carry out activities with peers to separate different types of mixtures.
sub_strands.values: Social justice: The learner gives others equal opportunities in sharing responsibilities as they carry out activities to separate heterogeneous mixtures.
sub_strands.pcis: Health Issues: The learner learns how to separate mixtures to remove impurities in cleaning of water for domestic usage as they carry out activities to demonstrate ways of separating mixtures.
sub_strands.links: Agriculture and Nutrition: The learner applies the knowledge on separating mixtures in agricultural processes like straining milk, winnowing grains and straining honey.

outcomes.text: classify mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous
apply appropriate methods to separate heterogeneous mixtures
outline the applications of separating mixtures in day-to-day life
appreciate different methods of separating mixtures in day-to-day life

skills.name: Explain what a mixture is
skills.mastery: The child says a mixture is two or more substances put together that are not joined chemically, so each keeps its own properties and can be separated again (sand and water, maize and beans, salt in water). The child knows that natural things such as air, soil and muddy river water are mixtures, and that the parts need not be in equal amounts. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the best meaning of a mixture
is this a mixture
can the parts be got back
which of these is not a mixture

prerequisites.reason: Substances in the three states of matter.

skills.name: Classify mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous
skills.mastery: The child says a mixture is homogeneous if it looks the same all through (salt or sugar dissolved in water, sweet tea without leaves, air) and heterogeneous if different parts can be seen (soil and water, sand and stones, maize and beans, oil and water). The child knows dissolved salt is still there, and that stirring does not make soil in water the same all through. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: sort a mixture into homogeneous or heterogeneous
pick the list that holds only heterogeneous mixtures
table of what can be seen: decide the type
why salty water is a mixture although it looks clear

prerequisites.reason: The child must know what a mixture is.

skills.name: Give examples of solid-solid, solid-liquid and liquid-liquid mixtures
skills.mastery: The child names the states of the parts of a mixture and gives examples of each type: solid-solid (maize and beans, sand and gravel), solid-liquid (sand and water, salt in water, tea leaves in tea) and liquid-liquid (oil and water, milk and water, vinegar and water). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what type is this mixture
pick the example of a liquid-liquid mixture
sort examples into the three types
name the states of the two parts

prerequisites.reason: Types of mixtures follow the meaning.
The child must know which things are solid and which are liquid.

skills.name: Choose the right method to separate a heterogeneous mixture
skills.mastery: Given a mixture from home or shamba, the child chooses the right method: winnowing (chaff from grain), picking (stones from rice or beans), sieving (bigger bits from flour or sand from stones), a magnet (iron nails or filings from sand), filtering (soil from muddy water), decanting (water from soil that has settled) or a separating funnel (oil from water). The child can say why the other methods do not suit. The hands-on part of the outcome needs a practical. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which method separates this mixture
match a mixture to a method
cause and effect: why a sieve will not separate salt from water
put the parts of the mixture and the method side by side in a table

prerequisites.reason: These methods are for heterogeneous mixtures.
Sorting things out of waste uses the same ideas.

skills.name: Explain why each separating method works
skills.mastery: The child gives the property each method uses: sieving uses the size of the pieces (small pieces fall through, big ones stay); winnowing uses weight (the wind blows the light chaff away and the heavier grain falls); filtering lets liquid through and keeps solid bits back but dissolved things go through too; decanting works when the solid has settled; a magnet works for iron. The child knows filtering does not remove dissolved salt or sugar. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what property does the method use
cause and effect: why the chaff is blown away
will filtering remove this
which part stays on the sieve

prerequisites.reason: The child names methods before explaining them.

skills.name: Outline how separating mixtures is used in daily life
skills.mastery: The child gives everyday uses of separating methods in Kenya: winnowing at harvest, sieving flour and sand for building, picking stones from rice and beans, filtering tea or water, a magnet picking iron from scrap at jua kali workshops, decanting settled water. The child knows these are done at home and at work, not only in a laboratory, and that filtering alone does not make water safe to drink. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which job uses this method
which of these is not an example of separating a mixture
match the job to the method
why a tea strainer is used

prerequisites.reason: Uses follow the methods.

misconceptions.error: Thinks that once substances are mixed they change into something new and cannot be got back.

example.question: Salt is stirred into water and seems to disappear. Can the salt be got back?
example.wrong_answer: No, the salt has gone for ever
example.correct_answer: Yes, the salt is still there and can be got back

misconceptions.cause: The child confuses mixing with cooking or burning, where new substances do form.
misconceptions.reveals: Use dissolving or sand and water and ask whether the parts are still there.
misconceptions.help: Leave salty water in the sun in a plate. The salt reappears as the water dries.
misconceptions.feedback: In a mixture each substance stays the same and can be separated again. Salty water dries and leaves the salt behind.
misconceptions.source: Prieto, Blanco and Rodriguez (1989), International Journal of Science Education; Longden, Black and Solomon (1991), International Journal of Science Education (children on dissolving). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a mixture must be made on purpose, so air, soil and muddy water are single things.

example.question: Is air a mixture?
example.wrong_answer: No, air is one substance
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is made of several gases

misconceptions.cause: The child links the word mixture with kitchen or classroom mixing.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask about air or soil and offer "one substance".
misconceptions.help: Look at soil in water: sand, clay and bits of plants settle in layers.
misconceptions.feedback: Mixtures can be natural. Air is a mixture of gases, and soil holds sand, clay and bits of plants.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the parts of a mixture must be in equal amounts.

example.question: Wafula puts one spoon of sand in a bucket of water. Is it a mixture?
example.wrong_answer: No, the parts are not equal
example.correct_answer: Yes, the parts can be in any amounts

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up mixtures with recipes that need fixed amounts.
misconceptions.reveals: Use very different amounts and offer "not a mixture".
misconceptions.help: Make three sand-and-water mixtures of different amounts and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: The parts of a mixture can be in any amounts. One spoon of sand in a bucket of water is still a mixture.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks dissolved salt or sugar has disappeared, so salty water is only water, not a mixture.

example.question: Is salt dissolved in water a mixture?
example.wrong_answer: No, the salt has disappeared so it is only water
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is a homogeneous mixture of salt and water

misconceptions.cause: The child cannot see the salt, so thinks it is gone.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a clear salt solution and offer "only water".
misconceptions.help: Taste the water, or let it dry to show the salt.
misconceptions.feedback: You cannot see the salt, but it is still there. Salty water is a mixture, and it looks the same all through, so it is homogeneous.
misconceptions.source: Prieto, Blanco and Rodriguez (1989), International Journal of Science Education; Longden, Black and Solomon (1991), International Journal of Science Education (children on dissolving). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a clear liquid must be pure, one substance only.

example.question: Sugar is dissolved in clear water. Is the water pure?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is clear
example.correct_answer: No, it is a mixture of sugar and water

misconceptions.cause: Clear and clean are used as the same word.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, it is clear" as a reason.
misconceptions.help: Taste the sugar water: clear but sweet.
misconceptions.feedback: Clear does not mean pure. Sweet or salty water is clear, but it holds sugar or salt too. It is a mixture.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks stirring makes any mixture the same all through (soil in water, oil in water).

example.question: Muddy water is stirred well. Is it homogeneous?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has been stirred it looks the same all through
example.correct_answer: No, the soil settles and different parts can be seen

misconceptions.cause: The child sees an even brown for a short time and calls it uniform.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a freshly stirred sand or soil mixture.
misconceptions.help: Stir soil in water and leave it for ten minutes. Layers form.
misconceptions.feedback: Stirred muddy water looks even for a short time, but the soil settles at the bottom. Different parts can be seen, so it is heterogeneous.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls salt dissolved in water a liquid-liquid mixture because it looks like liquid.

example.question: Salt is dissolved in water. What type of mixture is this?
example.wrong_answer: Liquid-liquid
example.correct_answer: Solid-liquid

misconceptions.cause: The child classifies by how the mixture looks after mixing, not by the states of the parts before.
misconceptions.reveals: Use dissolving examples and offer liquid-liquid.
misconceptions.help: Name the state of each part before they were mixed: salt (solid), water (liquid).
misconceptions.feedback: Look at the parts before they were mixed. Salt is a solid and water is a liquid, so this is a solid-liquid mixture.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a thick liquid (cooking oil, honey) is a solid.

example.question: Cooking oil is mixed with water. What type of mixture is this?
example.wrong_answer: Solid-liquid, because oil is thick
example.correct_answer: Liquid-liquid

misconceptions.cause: The child equates thick with solid.
misconceptions.reveals: Use oil, honey or milk and offer solid-liquid.
misconceptions.help: Pour oil: it flows and takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid.
misconceptions.feedback: Oil is thick but it flows and takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid. Oil and water make a liquid-liquid mixture.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks filtering separates any mixture, including dissolved salt or stones from rice.

example.question: Which method separates stones from rice?
example.wrong_answer: Filtering
example.correct_answer: Picking

misconceptions.cause: Filtering is the best-known method and the child uses it for everything.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer filtering for a dry solid-solid mixture.
misconceptions.help: Filter paper only works when one part is a liquid with solid bits in it. Try salt water on filter paper and taste the water.
misconceptions.feedback: Filtering is for solids mixed in a liquid. Stones in rice are both solids, so you pick them out or use a sieve.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a magnet picks up every metal (aluminium, copper, brass).

example.question: A jua kali worker has iron nails and aluminium bits mixed in a box. What can a magnet pick out?
example.wrong_answer: Both the nails and the aluminium bits
example.correct_answer: Only the iron nails

misconceptions.cause: The child has learned "magnets pick up metals" and has not tested different metals.
misconceptions.reveals: Mix an iron item with aluminium or copper and ask what the magnet takes.
misconceptions.help: Test an iron nail, an aluminium sufuria piece and a copper wire with a magnet.
misconceptions.feedback: A magnet picks up iron and steel, not every metal. Aluminium and copper are not picked up.
misconceptions.source: Common test of children's ideas about magnets (D94). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a separating funnel separates a solid from a liquid.

example.question: Which mixture is separated with a separating funnel?
example.wrong_answer: Sand and water
example.correct_answer: Cooking oil and water

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the funnel is for liquids and does not know it needs two liquids that do not mix.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer sand and water for a funnel.
misconceptions.help: Pour oil and water in a funnel and open the tap: the water comes first. Try sand and water and see that it is not suited.
misconceptions.feedback: A separating funnel is for two liquids that do not mix, such as oil and water. The lower liquid is let out through the tap.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks filtering removes dissolved salt or sugar from water.

example.question: Salty water is poured through filter paper. What is in the water that comes through?
example.wrong_answer: Only water, the filter keeps the salt back
example.correct_answer: Water and the dissolved salt

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the paper catches everything that is not water.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what drips through filter paper after salt solution and offer "only water".
misconceptions.help: Filter salty water and taste it. It is still salty. Boil it down to see the salt.
misconceptions.feedback: Dissolved salt is in tiny pieces that pass through the paper with the water. Filtering only keeps back bits too big to pass through, such as soil.
misconceptions.source: Prieto, Blanco and Rodriguez (1989), International Journal of Science Education; Longden, Black and Solomon (1991), International Journal of Science Education (children on dissolving). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks that in winnowing the wind blows the heavy grain away and the light chaff stays.

example.question: When grain is winnowed, what does the wind blow away?
example.wrong_answer: The heavier grain
example.correct_answer: The lighter chaff

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen the activity but not tied the result to weight.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what the wind blows away and offer the grain.
misconceptions.help: Drop a coin and a feather in front of a fan to see which one is blown away.
misconceptions.feedback: The wind blows away the lighter chaff. The heavier grain falls straight down into the basin.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the small pieces stay on the sieve and the big ones fall through.

example.question: Maize flour with husks is passed through a sieve. What stays on the sieve?
example.wrong_answer: The fine flour
example.correct_answer: The big husks

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of the sieve as a net that catches little things.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what stays in the sieve and offer the fine flour.
misconceptions.help: Sieve sand and small stones and look at what remains.
misconceptions.feedback: The holes of a sieve let small pieces fall through. Pieces too big for the holes stay on top.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks separating mixtures is only done in a science laboratory.

example.question: Where do people separate mixtures?
example.wrong_answer: Only in a science laboratory
example.correct_answer: At home, in the shamba and at work as well as in a laboratory

misconceptions.cause: The child connects science words with the lab.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask where mixtures are separated and offer "only in a laboratory".
misconceptions.help: List the actions a family does in a day: sieve flour, pick stones from beans, strain tea.
misconceptions.feedback: People separate mixtures every day: sieving flour, picking stones from beans, straining tea, winnowing grain.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks filtering muddy water makes it safe to drink.

example.question: Muddy water is filtered through a clean cloth. Is the water now safe to drink?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it looks clean
example.correct_answer: No, germs and dissolved things can still be in it

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that clear means safe.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask whether filtered water is safe and offer "yes".
misconceptions.help: Remember: germs are too small to be caught by a cloth. The water must also be boiled or treated.
misconceptions.feedback: Filtering takes out the bits you can see, but germs and dissolved things are still there. The water must also be boiled or treated.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

Outcome b ("apply ... methods") has a hands-on half (carrying out the separation) that needs a practical; the questions test choosing the method and explaining why it works.
