outcomes.text: identify water pollutants in the water sources
outline the effects of water pollution in day-to-day life
identify methods of reducing water pollution in the water sources
apply appropriate methods of water treatment
advocate for safe water sources in the locality

skills.name: Identify pollutants in water sources
skills.mastery: The child names common water pollutants and where they come from: sewage and waste from latrines and drains, plastic and rubbish, oil and petrol from garages and boats, soap and detergent from washing, fertiliser and pesticide washed from shambas, waste from factories, and animal dung. The child knows water can be polluted even when it looks clear, and that households and farms pollute too, not only factories. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which of these pollutes a river
sort things into pollutants and not pollutants
where does this pollutant come from
which source is a polluter that is not a factory

prerequisites.reason: Water sources and conservation were met in Grade 4.
Dangers of waste link to water pollution.

skills.name: Outline the effects of water pollution
skills.mastery: The child gives effects on people (diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid and other water-borne diseases, bad taste and smell, costs of treating water), on animals (fish and other animals die or get ill) and on plants (crops and water plants die), and says pollution travels downstream and harms people far from where it was dumped. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the effect that is true
cause and effect: what happens to the fish
who is harmed downstream
which is not an effect of polluted water

prerequisites.reason: The child must know the pollutants first.

skills.name: Identify ways of reducing water pollution
skills.mastery: The child gives ways of reducing pollution at a water source: do not dump rubbish or waste in water, wash clothes and cars away from the river and pour the dirty water on the ground, dig latrines far from wells and rivers, use fewer chemicals on the shamba, plant trees and grass along the river banks, and report spills. Dilution by a big river is not a solution. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which action helps keep a river clean
which action pollutes
cause and effect: where to dig a latrine
what to do with dirty washing water

prerequisites.reason: Prevention depends on the sources.

skills.name: Choose an appropriate method of water treatment
skills.mastery: Given a water problem, the child chooses the method and the right order: let it settle and filter muddy water first; boil to kill germs; add chlorine or water-treatment tablets in the correct amount; or leave clear water in a clear plastic bottle in strong sun for about six hours (solar treatment). The child knows each method does one job: boiling does not remove chemicals or dirt, filtering does not kill germs, and muddy water must be filtered before solar or chemical treatment. The practical part needs a hands-on lesson. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which method fits this problem
put the steps of treating muddy water in order
cause and effect: why filter before adding chlorine
which method does not make this water safe

prerequisites.reason: Filtering and settling are separating methods.
The child knows why untreated water is a danger.

misconceptions.error: Thinks water is polluted only if dirt can be seen, so clear water is clean.

example.question: The water in a stream looks clear. Does that mean it is not polluted?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, clear water cannot be polluted
example.correct_answer: No, germs and chemicals cannot be seen

misconceptions.cause: The child uses looks as the test for clean water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "clear water is clean" as an answer.
misconceptions.help: Dissolve soap or salt in a glass of water: it is clear but not clean to drink.
misconceptions.feedback: Germs and many chemicals cannot be seen. Clear water can still be polluted.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only factories pollute water.

example.question: Which of these can pollute a river?
example.wrong_answer: Only a factory pipe
example.correct_answer: A factory pipe, washing at the river and a latrine near the bank

misconceptions.cause: The child links pollution with big machines and smoke.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "only factories" and list home sources.
misconceptions.help: Make a map of the school stream and list every source of waste along it.
misconceptions.feedback: Homes, shambas and schools pollute water too: soap, rubbish, dung, fertiliser and latrines near the water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks useful things such as soap and fertiliser cannot pollute water.

example.question: Fertiliser helps maize grow. Can it pollute a river?
example.wrong_answer: No, it helps plants so it cannot harm water
example.correct_answer: Yes, rain can wash it into the river and it harms living things there

misconceptions.cause: The child links useful with harmless.
misconceptions.reveals: Use fertiliser, soap or pesticide and offer "cannot pollute".
misconceptions.help: Look at a pond green with algae after too much fertiliser washed into it.
misconceptions.feedback: Useful things pollute water when they get into it in the wrong place. Fertiliser and soap washed into a river harm the living things there.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks polluted water harms only people, not animals and plants.

example.question: Oil spills into a river. What happens to the fish?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, pollution only harms people
example.correct_answer: Many fish may die or fall ill

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of dirty water as a danger to drinkers.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask about fish or crops and offer "nothing".
misconceptions.help: Look at pictures of an oil spill near a shore.
misconceptions.feedback: Pollution harms plants and animals as well as people. Fish can die when the water is polluted.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks pollution harms only the place where it was dumped, not people downstream.

example.question: A factory dumps waste into a river. Who may be harmed?
example.wrong_answer: Only people next to the factory
example.correct_answer: People and animals living further down the river

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures pollution as staying put.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask who is harmed and offer "only the place where it was dumped".
misconceptions.help: Put food colouring in a gutter model and watch it travel.
misconceptions.feedback: A river carries pollution with the water. People and animals far downstream can be harmed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks polluted water is only a problem if it smells or tastes bad.

example.question: Water from a stream has no smell and no bad taste. Is it safe to drink?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it has no smell or taste
example.correct_answer: Not necessarily, it can have germs that cause diarrhoea

misconceptions.cause: The child uses smell and taste as the test.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "smells fine, so safe".
misconceptions.help: Remember that cholera germs have no smell.
misconceptions.feedback: Germs have no taste or smell. Water can look and taste fine and still make you ill.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a big river washes waste away, so a little rubbish does not matter.

example.question: Kamau says "The river is big, so one bag of rubbish does no harm." What is wrong with this?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, a big river washes it away
example.correct_answer: The waste does not disappear; it spreads and harms people and animals downstream

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that carrying away is the same as making harmless.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the river is big" as an answer.
misconceptions.help: Show a bucket of coloured water poured into a larger bucket: the colour only spreads.
misconceptions.feedback: A river does not make waste disappear. It carries it away to other places, where it still harms.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a latrine close to a well or river is fine.

example.question: Where is the best place to dig a latrine?
example.wrong_answer: Next to the well, so it is easy to reach
example.correct_answer: Far from the well and the river

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of convenience, not of how water moves through the soil.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer a place close to the water.
misconceptions.help: Pour coloured water through soil near a model well.
misconceptions.feedback: Waste from a latrine can seep through the soil into wells and rivers. It must be dug far from them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks washing clothes or cars in the river is harmless.

example.question: Where should a family wash clothes to keep a stream clean?
example.wrong_answer: In the stream, because the soap washes away
example.correct_answer: Away from the stream, pouring the used water on the ground

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the river as the easiest place for the job.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer washing in the stream.
misconceptions.help: Ask what is in used wash water: soap, oil and dirt.
misconceptions.feedback: Soap and dirt harm fish and make the water unsafe for others. Wash at home and pour the used water on the ground.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks filtering water makes it safe to drink.

example.question: A family filters stream water through cloth. What must they still do before drinking it?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, filtering makes it safe
example.correct_answer: Boil it or treat it to kill germs

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that clear means safe and that filters kill germs.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what to do after filtering and offer "nothing".
misconceptions.help: Compare the water under a microscope picture: germs are far smaller than the holes in cloth.
misconceptions.feedback: Filtering removes bits you can see. It does not kill germs. The water must be boiled or treated as well.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks boiling removes dirt and chemicals from water.

example.question: Water polluted with soap and oil is boiled. Is it now safe to drink?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, boiling removes everything harmful
example.correct_answer: No, boiling kills germs but does not remove soap or oil

misconceptions.cause: The child sees boiling as the cure for all water problems.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer boiling for a chemical problem.
misconceptions.help: Boil salty water: it is still salty.
misconceptions.feedback: Boiling kills germs. It does not take out chemicals, soap or oil.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks muddy water can be treated in the sun in a bucket without filtering.

example.question: Which water is suitable for solar treatment in a clear plastic bottle?
example.wrong_answer: Muddy water straight from the river
example.correct_answer: Water that has been left to settle and filtered until it is clear

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know that mud blocks the sun's rays and shields germs.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer muddy water for solar treatment.
misconceptions.help: Place two bottles in the sun: one clear and one muddy.
misconceptions.feedback: Sunlight must reach the germs. Muddy water blocks the light, so it must be settled and filtered first.
misconceptions.source: Solar disinfection guidance (SODIS) commonly requires clear water. To confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks more chlorine makes the water safer.

example.question: A mother adds three times the amount of water treatment tablet shown on the packet. What is the problem?
example.wrong_answer: None, more chlorine makes it safer
example.correct_answer: Too much chlorine makes the water taste bad and can harm people; the packet amount should be used

misconceptions.cause: The child believes more of a cleaning thing is always better.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "more is safer".
misconceptions.help: Read the packet instructions together.
misconceptions.feedback: Use exactly the amount on the packet. Too much chlorine gives a bad taste and can make you ill.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome e ("advocate for safe water sources in the locality") is an attitude and action outcome: no question family; it needs a project (a campaign or a survey of the local water source). outcomes.text: classify objects as floating or sinking in water
identify factors that affect floating and sinking of objects in water
explain applications of floating and sinking in day-to-day life
appreciate the use of floaters as life savers

skills.name: Classify objects as floating or sinking in water
skills.mastery: Given an everyday object (cork, dry wood, a leaf, an empty plastic bottle, a coin, a stone, a nail, a key, a sponge, a bar of soap, an unpeeled orange), the child says whether it floats or sinks in water and does not decide by weight alone, size alone or the material name alone. A big log floats; a small stone sinks. The practical part (testing objects) needs a hands-on lesson. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: will this object float or sink
pick the list that holds only floating objects
read a table of results and decide
which one of these will sink

prerequisites.reason: Properties of solids and liquids.
Knowing the gramme helps in reading mass in the results tables.

skills.name: Identify the factors that affect floating and sinking
skills.mastery: The child says that shape, weight and size together decide whether an object floats: a ball of clay sinks, but the same clay made into a bowl floats because it pushes aside more water; a heavy object floats if it is big and light for its size; adding a load to a floating object makes it float lower, and too much load makes it sink. Given a results table of objects of the same size, the child reads which factor is changed. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what changed so the object floats
read a table: which factor is different
cause and effect: what happens when too many people get into a canoe
which change makes a floating object sink

prerequisites.reason: Floating and sinking must be known first.
Reading a table of results.
Comparing masses in grammes.

skills.name: Explain how floating and sinking are used in daily life
skills.mastery: The child explains uses of floating and sinking: life jackets and floats keep people up because they are light for their size; ships and boats are shaped to push aside a lot of water; fishing nets use floats and sinkers; a water tank float valve rises with the water level; swimmers use floats. The child knows a floating thing still has weight. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: why does a life jacket keep you up
why does a steel ship float
which object is a float and which a sinker
match the object to its use

prerequisites.reason: Applications follow the factors.

misconceptions.error: Thinks heavy things sink and light things float.

example.question: A big wooden log is much heavier than a small stone. Which one sinks?
example.wrong_answer: The log, because it is heavier
example.correct_answer: The stone, even though it is lighter

misconceptions.cause: The child uses weight alone, the quality that is easy to feel in the hand.
misconceptions.reveals: Pair a heavy floater (log) with a light sinker (small stone or nail).
misconceptions.help: Drop a big log and a small stone in water. Repeat with a coin and a leaf.
misconceptions.feedback: Weight alone does not decide. A heavy log floats and a small stone sinks. What matters is how heavy the object is for its size.
misconceptions.source: Kohn (1993), Preschoolers' reasoning about density: will it float?, Child Development; Hsin and Wu (2011), Journal of Science Education and Technology; Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a material always floats or always sinks: all metal sinks, all wood floats.

example.question: A steel ship is made of metal. Does it float or sink?
example.wrong_answer: It sinks, because all metal sinks
example.correct_answer: It floats

misconceptions.cause: The child has learned a rule from a few objects and applies it to every object of that material.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a metal that floats (a tin bowl, a ship) or a wood that sinks (ebony).
misconceptions.help: Float a tin lid on its flat side, then push it under so it fills with water.
misconceptions.feedback: The material alone does not decide. A metal ship floats because of its shape, and a piece of ebony wood sinks. Test each object.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an object that sinks in a basin would float in a lake because there is more water.

example.question: A stone sinks in a bucket of water. What happens if it is dropped in a deep lake?
example.wrong_answer: It floats, because the lake is deeper
example.correct_answer: It sinks, the same as in the bucket

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that more water holds things up more.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "floats in deep water".
misconceptions.help: Drop the stone in a shallow dish and in a bucket. The result is the same.
misconceptions.feedback: The amount of water does not change the result. A stone that sinks in a bucket sinks in a lake.
misconceptions.source: Hsin and Wu (2011) report children citing the depth of water. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks shape makes no difference: a ball of clay sinks, so a bowl of the same clay sinks too.

example.question: A ball of clay sinks. The same clay is made into a bowl shape. What happens?
example.wrong_answer: It still sinks, because it is the same clay
example.correct_answer: It can float, because the bowl shape pushes aside more water

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of the material and mass only.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a same-material pair with two shapes and offer "no change".
misconceptions.help: Float a foil boat and then crumple the same foil into a ball.
misconceptions.feedback: The same clay can float or sink depending on its shape. A bowl pushes aside more water, so it can float.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only weight decides, so a heavier object always sinks.

example.question: Two blocks have the same size. Block A is heavier than block B. Which is more likely to sink?
example.wrong_answer: Both float the same way
example.correct_answer: Block A, which is heavier for its size

misconceptions.cause: The child ignores size when it is the same, or ignores weight when it is not.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a same-size pair and offer "same result".
misconceptions.help: Compare two cups of the same size filled with sand and with cotton.
misconceptions.feedback: For objects of the same size, the heavier one is more likely to sink. Weight and size must be thought about together.
misconceptions.source: Kohn (1993); Hsin and Wu (2011). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks bigger pieces of the same material sink and smaller ones float (or the other way round).

example.question: A small piece of dry wood floats. Will a much bigger piece of the same wood float?
example.wrong_answer: No, it is too big
example.correct_answer: Yes, it floats too

misconceptions.cause: The child uses size alone.
misconceptions.reveals: Compare big and small pieces of one material.
misconceptions.help: Float a splinter and a log of the same wood.
misconceptions.feedback: Size alone does not decide. Big and small pieces of the same wood both float, because the wood is light for its size.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks adding a load to a floating object makes no difference.

example.question: More and more people climb into a small canoe on Lake Victoria. What happens?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing changes, it floats just as high
example.correct_answer: It floats lower and lower and can sink

misconceptions.cause: The child has no idea of the push of water having a limit.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a canoe or a boat with passengers.
misconceptions.help: Add stones one by one to a floating plastic tub and watch it sink lower.
misconceptions.feedback: Each added load makes the boat float lower. With too much load water comes over the side and it sinks.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a steel ship floats because steel is lighter than water.

example.question: Why does a huge steel ship float?
example.wrong_answer: Because steel is lighter than water
example.correct_answer: Because its shape pushes aside a lot of water

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks floating means the material is light.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask why the ship floats and offer "steel is light".
misconceptions.help: A steel nail sinks. Shape the same steel into a bowl and it floats.
misconceptions.feedback: Steel is heavier than water. A ship floats because it is shaped like a big hollow bowl that pushes aside a lot of water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks floating things weigh nothing.

example.question: A floating log is lifted out of the water onto a scale. What does the scale show?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, because floating things have no weight
example.correct_answer: Its weight, as the log is heavy

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks "not sinking" means "not heavy".
misconceptions.reveals: Ask about the weight of a floating thing.
misconceptions.help: Weigh a block of wood that floats.
misconceptions.feedback: A floating object still has weight. It floats because the water pushes it up.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome d ("appreciate the use of floaters as life savers") is attitudinal: no question family. Outcomes a and b are practical investigations in the design; the questions test the results and reasoning, not the handling of the objects.

Effects of loud sound.

outcomes.text: identify sources of sound in nature
demonstrate the movement of sound in nature
describe effects of loud sound in day-to-day life
appreciate the role of sound in day-to-day life

skills.name: Identify sources of sound and what makes sound
skills.mastery: The child names sources of sound in nature and daily life (drum, guitar or nyatiti string, flute and whistle, voice, bees, thunder, a hit tin) and says all sounds are made by something vibrating (moving quickly to and fro): a drum skin, a string, the air in a pipe or the voice box. The child knows that plucking, blowing and banging can all make sound. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what is vibrating in this instrument
which of these makes a sound without being hit
pick the true statement about sound
what we can feel on the throat when we hum

prerequisites.reason: Force moving things to and fro.

skills.name: Describe how sound moves in nature
skills.mastery: The child says that sound travels as vibrations through solids, liquids and gases, in all directions from the source; that it needs something to travel through, so there is no sound in space; that it travels faster through solids and water than through air; that loudness does not change its speed; and that an echo is sound bouncing back. Lightning is seen before thunder is heard because light travels much faster than sound. The demonstration part needs a hands-on lesson. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: through which material does sound travel fastest
can sound travel in space
why thunder comes after lightning
cause and effect: why you can hear someone through a closed wooden door

prerequisites.reason: Sound is made by vibrations; travel is how they spread.
Solids, liquids and gases.

skills.name: Describe the effects of loud sound in daily life
skills.mastery: The child describes effects of loud sound: damage to hearing (even loss of hearing), headaches, stress and poor sleep, difficulty learning, and fright for animals; and ways to protect hearing (ear protection for workers, keeping music and matatu speakers low, moving away from the noise). The child knows that being used to a noise does not make it harmless and that loud music can harm too. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which is an effect of very loud sound
what protects hearing
cause and effect: a worker near a loud machine
which of these is not a good way to protect hearing

prerequisites.reason: Knowing how sound is made helps the child see why very strong vibrations harm.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sound is made without anything moving, or that the sound is "in" the object.

example.question: What happens to the skin of a drum when it makes a sound?
example.wrong_answer: It stays still; the sound is inside the drum
example.correct_answer: It vibrates, moving quickly to and fro

misconceptions.cause: The child cannot see the vibration and thinks nothing moves.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what the drum skin does and offer "stays still".
misconceptions.help: Put rice grains on a drum and hit it: they jump. Hold a ruler off the edge of a desk and twang it.
misconceptions.feedback: Every sound is made by something vibrating. The drum skin moves quickly to and fro, and the rice on it jumps.
misconceptions.source: Eshach and Schwartz (2006), Sound stuff? Naive materialism in middle-school students' conceptions of sound, International Journal of Science Education. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks that in a flute or whistle the air is not part of the sound, only the instrument.

example.question: What vibrates to make the sound in a flute?
example.wrong_answer: The metal or wood of the flute only
example.correct_answer: The air inside the flute

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the instrument as the object that moves.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what vibrates in a flute and offer the flute itself.
misconceptions.help: Blow across the top of a bottle and change the water level.
misconceptions.feedback: In a flute or whistle the air inside the pipe vibrates. The vibrating air makes the sound.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sound is only made by hitting or banging things.

example.question: Which action can make a sound from a string?
example.wrong_answer: Only hitting it with a stick
example.correct_answer: Plucking it with a finger

misconceptions.cause: The child has met drums and bells mostly.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer hitting as the only way.
misconceptions.help: Pluck a stretched rubber band, then blow across a bottle: sound without banging.
misconceptions.feedback: Sound can come from plucking, blowing, rubbing or banging. What matters is that something vibrates.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sound travels only through air, not through water or solids.

example.question: A learner puts an ear to a wooden desk while a friend taps the other end. What happens?
example.wrong_answer: She hears nothing, because sound only travels through air
example.correct_answer: She hears the tap clearly, because sound travels through the wood

misconceptions.cause: The child associates sound with the air they live in.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a solid or water and offer "only air".
misconceptions.help: Tap a desk and listen with the ear on it. Swimmers hear sounds under water.
misconceptions.feedback: Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases. It can even go through wood and water.
misconceptions.source: Eshach and Schwartz (2006); Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sound travels through space.

example.question: An astronaut outside a spacecraft shouts. Can another astronaut far away hear it?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, sound travels everywhere
example.correct_answer: No, there is no air or other material in space to carry the sound

misconceptions.cause: Films show explosions in space with sound.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask whether space can carry sound and offer "yes".
misconceptions.help: Ring a bell in a jar with the air pumped out (video). It goes quiet.
misconceptions.feedback: Sound needs something to travel through, such as air, water or a solid. Space is empty, so sound cannot travel there.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sound travels faster through air than through solids or water.

example.question: Through which material does sound travel fastest?
example.wrong_answer: Air
example.correct_answer: Steel

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that lighter materials let things travel faster.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer air as the fastest.
misconceptions.help: Listen to a train through a rail and through the air.
misconceptions.feedback: Sound travels fastest through solids such as steel, slower through water and slowest through air.
misconceptions.source: Eshach and Schwartz (2006) report this reversal. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a louder sound travels faster than a quiet one.

example.question: Two drums are played, one very loud and one very quiet, at the same distance. Which sound arrives first?
example.wrong_answer: The louder one
example.correct_answer: They arrive at the same time

misconceptions.cause: The child links loud with strong and strong with quick.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the louder one".
misconceptions.help: Watch a band at a distance: loud and quiet notes of the same beat arrive together.
misconceptions.feedback: Loudness does not change speed. The sound from a loud drum and a quiet drum take the same time to arrive.
misconceptions.source: Wittmann, Steinberg and Redish (1999) on students' ideas about wave speed. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks loud sound affects only the ears, and only for a short time.

example.question: Which problems can very loud noise cause?
example.wrong_answer: It only makes the ears ring for a moment
example.correct_answer: Damage to hearing, headaches and poor sleep

misconceptions.cause: The child has felt ringing ears after a loud noise and thinks that is all.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask what loud noise can cause and offer the short ringing.
misconceptions.help: Ask the class how they feel after a long day in a very noisy place.
misconceptions.feedback: Very loud sound can damage hearing for good. It can also cause headaches, stress and poor sleep.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks that being used to a loud noise means it no longer harms.

example.question: A boda boda rider has driven near loud engines for years and says he is now used to the noise. What is true?
example.wrong_answer: Because he is used to it, the noise cannot harm his hearing
example.correct_answer: His hearing can still be getting damaged even if the noise no longer bothers him

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that feeling no discomfort means no harm.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "used to it, so no harm".
misconceptions.help: Explain that the tiny hair cells in the ear are not renewed once damaged.
misconceptions.feedback: Feeling used to a noise does not stop the damage. Loud noise can still harm hearing, so ear protection is needed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks loud music cannot harm hearing because it is pleasant.

example.question: A matatu plays music at full volume every day. What is true for the passengers?
example.wrong_answer: It cannot harm them, because music is pleasant
example.correct_answer: It can harm their hearing, because any very loud sound can

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks that "noise" means only unpleasant sounds.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "music cannot harm".
misconceptions.help: Ask what happens to the ears at a very loud concert.
misconceptions.feedback: It is the loudness, not the kind of sound, that harms. Very loud music can damage hearing as well.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome d ("appreciate the role of sound in day-to-day life") is attitudinal: no question family. Outcome b ("demonstrate the movement of sound") is a practical (string telephone, tapping a desk): the questions test the reasoning only.

perform experiments to demonstrate the modes of heat transfer,
carry out experiments to identify good and poor conductors of heat,
discuss with peers applications of heat transfer in day-to-day life (cooking, melting, freezing, maintaining body temperature, insulation),
use digital or print media to search for applications of heat transfer in day-to-day life,

sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: The learner displays self-confidence as they perform experiments to demonstrate the modes of heat transfer.
sub_strands.values: Social justice: The learner practices sharing of resources equitably as they perform experiments to identify good and poor conductors of heat.

outcomes.text: demonstrate the modes of heat transfer in nature
classify conductors of heat into good or poor conductors
explain the uses of heat transfer in day-to-day life
acknowledge safety precautions when handling heat

skills.name: Name the modes of heat transfer: conduction, convection and radiation
skills.mastery: The child matches each mode to an example: conduction (heat moving along a solid or from one solid to another that touches it, such as a spoon in hot tea or a sufuria on a jiko); convection (heat carried by moving hot liquid or air, such as boiling water or smoke going up); radiation (heat travelling without anything to carry it, such as the sun warming the Earth or a fire warming you at a distance). The child knows heat moves from a hotter place to a colder place, and that it is hot air, not heat, that rises. The demonstration part needs a hands-on lesson. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which mode is this example
how does the sun's heat reach the Earth
why smoke goes up
put the way heat moves along a metal rod in order

prerequisites.reason: Sources of heat were met in Grade 4.
Uses of heat in daily life.

skills.name: Classify materials as good or poor conductors of heat
skills.mastery: The child says which materials are good conductors (metals such as aluminium, iron, copper) and which are poor conductors, also called insulators (wood, plastic, cloth, wool, air, clay), and why a metal object feels colder than a wooden one at the same temperature (it takes heat away from the hand faster). The child knows wool and blankets keep us warm by holding in body heat, not by making heat. The practical part needs a hands-on lesson. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: good or poor conductor
pick the list that holds only good conductors
table of how fast an object heated: which is a poor conductor
why a metal chair feels colder than a wooden one

prerequisites.reason: Conduction is the mode that conductors carry.
Reading a table of results.

skills.name: Explain the uses of heat transfer in daily life
skills.mastery: The child explains uses of heat transfer at home and at work: metal sufurias and wooden spoons (mwiko) for cooking; iron sheet roofs and ceilings; vents high in a room or a kitchen so hot air and smoke go out by convection; drying clothes and maize in the sun (radiation); white or light-coloured surfaces stay cooler than dark ones in the sun; a flask or a thick wall keeps heat in or out. Each use is named with its mode. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which mode explains this use
why is the vent near the roof
which colour keeps a room cooler
match the use to the material

prerequisites.reason: Uses name the modes.
Uses of conductors and insulators.

skills.name: Know the safety precautions when handling heat
skills.mastery: The child chooses safe ways of handling hot things: use a dry cloth or pot holder, hold wooden or plastic handles, keep children away from fire and hot water, turn pan handles inwards, never touch a pot that has just come off the fire even if no flame shows, and keep the jiko in a ventilated place. The attitude half of outcome d (acknowledging) is shown by behaviour and cannot be tested by typing. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which is the safest way to lift a hot sufuria
which action is unsafe
cause and effect: why a wet cloth is dangerous
what to do when a pot is just off the fire

prerequisites.reason: Grade 4 outcome on safety measures when using heat.
Conductors explain which handles to hold.

misconceptions.error: Thinks heat itself rises, so heat can only go upwards.

example.question: A hot metal rod is held sideways. In which direction does the heat spread?
example.wrong_answer: Only upwards, because heat rises
example.correct_answer: Along the rod, away from the hot end, in every direction

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard "heat rises" and turns it into a rule about all heat.
misconceptions.reveals: Use a sideways or downward situation and offer "up only".
misconceptions.help: Hold a lit candle under, beside and over your hand and feel the warmth in all of them.
misconceptions.feedback: Hot air rises, but heat is not limited to going up. In a solid, heat spreads along it from the hot end to the colder parts.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge; Erickson (1979), Children's conceptions of heat and temperature, Science Education. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks cold flows from ice or a cold object into a warm one.

example.question: A cold drink is held in a warm hand. What is moving?
example.wrong_answer: Cold moves from the drink into the hand
example.correct_answer: Heat moves from the hand into the drink

misconceptions.cause: The child feels the cold and thinks something cold is arriving.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "cold flows into the hand".
misconceptions.help: Put a thermometer in the hand and then on the bottle.
misconceptions.feedback: There is no flow of cold. Heat always moves from a warmer thing to a colder thing, so the hand loses heat to the drink.
misconceptions.source: Erickson (1979); Wiser and Carey (1983). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the sun's heat reaches us by conduction through air, or needs air to travel.

example.question: Space between the Sun and the Earth is empty. How does the Sun's heat reach us?
example.wrong_answer: By conduction through the air
example.correct_answer: By radiation, which needs nothing to carry it

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures heat as needing something to travel through, like sound.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask how the sun's heat arrives and offer conduction.
misconceptions.help: Hold a hand near a lit lamp and feel the warmth without touching.
misconceptions.feedback: Radiation is heat that travels without anything to carry it. That is how the Sun's heat crosses empty space.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks convection can happen in solids, such as along a metal spoon.

example.question: Which mode moves heat along a metal spoon placed in hot tea?
example.wrong_answer: Convection
example.correct_answer: Conduction

misconceptions.cause: The child has memorised the names and cannot tell which fits which material.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer convection for a solid.
misconceptions.help: Convection needs a fluid that can move. A spoon cannot move its particles around.
misconceptions.feedback: Convection happens only in liquids and gases that can flow. Heat moves along a solid by conduction.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks metal is colder than wood or plastic because it feels colder.

example.question: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same room all night. Which one is colder?
example.wrong_answer: The metal spoon, because it feels colder
example.correct_answer: Neither, they are the same temperature

misconceptions.cause: The child uses the feeling in the hand as the temperature.
misconceptions.reveals: Use two things left in the same room and offer "metal is colder".
misconceptions.help: Measure both with a thermometer: the reading is the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Both are at the temperature of the room. Metal feels colder because it takes heat away from your hand faster.
misconceptions.source: Erickson (1979); Wiser and Carey (1983); Harrison, Grayson and Treagust (1999). Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks wool and blankets make heat of their own.

example.question: A cold child is wrapped in a woollen blanket. Where does the warmth come from?
example.wrong_answer: The blanket makes heat
example.correct_answer: The child's own body, kept in by the blanket

misconceptions.cause: The child feels warmth and credits the thing wrapped around.
misconceptions.reveals: Put a thermometer in a blanket alone and offer "the blanket makes heat".
misconceptions.help: Wrap a thermometer in a blanket: the temperature does not rise. Wrap a warm bottle and watch it stay warm.
misconceptions.feedback: A blanket is a poor conductor. It keeps your own heat in, but it makes no heat. A blanket around a thermometer does not make it warmer.
misconceptions.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a good conductor of heat keeps heat in for a long time.

example.question: Which pot handle is better for a hot sufuria?
example.wrong_answer: Metal, because metal holds heat in
example.correct_answer: Wood, because it does not carry heat to the hand

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up carrying heat (conducting) with keeping heat in.
misconceptions.reveals: Ask which handle is safe and offer metal.
misconceptions.help: Put a metal and a wooden spoon in hot water and feel the handles after a minute.
misconceptions.feedback: A good conductor carries heat quickly, so a metal handle gets hot too. A poor conductor such as wood keeps the heat from your hand.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the colour of a surface makes no difference to how hot it gets in the sun.

example.question: Two iron sheet roofs, one painted white and one painted black, stand in the sun. Which gets hotter?
example.wrong_answer: Both the same, colour makes no difference
example.correct_answer: The black one, as dark surfaces take in more of the sun's heat

misconceptions.cause: The child has not compared surfaces in the sun.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the same".
misconceptions.help: Put a white and a black tin in the sun with thermometers.
misconceptions.feedback: Dark surfaces take in more of the sun's radiation and get hotter. Light surfaces reflect more and stay cooler.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks air vents for a hot room or kitchen are best low on the wall, because heat goes down.

example.question: Why is a vent put near the roof of a hot kitchen?
example.wrong_answer: Heat goes downwards, so the vent has to catch it
example.correct_answer: Hot air and smoke rise, so they go out through the vent at the top

misconceptions.cause: The child has not met convection in air.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer a vent near the floor as correct.
misconceptions.help: Hold a candle flame near the top and bottom of a doorway and see the smoke go.
misconceptions.feedback: Hot air is lighter and rises, so smoke and hot air can leave through a high vent. This is convection.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks heat transfer matters only when cooking.

example.question: Which of these uses heat transfer?
example.wrong_answer: Only cooking uses it
example.correct_answer: Cooking, drying clothes in the sun and a flask that keeps tea hot all use it

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of heat in the kitchen only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "only cooking".
misconceptions.help: List the places in a day where heat moves: sun on the roof, tea cooling, wearing a jumper.
misconceptions.feedback: Heat moves everywhere: when we cook, dry clothes in the sun and keep tea hot in a flask.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a wet cloth is the safest thing to hold a hot sufuria with.

example.question: Wanjiru needs to lift a hot sufuria. Which cloth is safest to use?
example.wrong_answer: A wet cloth, because water cools it
example.correct_answer: A dry, thick cloth

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks water always cools things.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer a wet cloth.
misconceptions.help: A wet cloth conducts heat and steam burns. Compare a dry and a wet cloth on a warm tin.
misconceptions.feedback: A wet cloth conducts heat to your hand and makes steam, which burns. Use a thick dry cloth.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a pot that is no longer on the fire, or has no flame or steam, is safe to touch.

example.question: A sufuria has just been taken off the jiko. There is no flame or steam. Is it safe to touch?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, there is no flame or steam so it is cool
example.correct_answer: No, it can stay hot for a long time

misconceptions.cause: The child uses flame or steam as the sign of heat.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no flame so cool".
misconceptions.help: Hold a hand near, not on, the pot and feel the heat.
misconceptions.feedback: Metal can stay very hot for a long time even when there is no flame or steam. Do not touch it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a metal handle on a hot pan is safe because metal is strong.

example.question: A sufuria has a metal handle. What is the danger when it is on the fire?
example.wrong_answer: None, metal is strong and safe
example.correct_answer: The handle gets hot because metal carries heat to it

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up strong with safe.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "none".
misconceptions.help: Put a metal and a wooden spoon in hot water and feel both handles.
misconceptions.feedback: Metal is a good conductor, so the handle becomes hot too. Always use a dry cloth to hold a metal handle.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome a ("demonstrate the modes of heat transfer") and b (classifying conductors) are practicals in the design; the questions test the reasoning. Outcome d ("acknowledge safety precautions") is half attitude: the knowledge half has a skill (HEAT_SAFETY); the acknowledging is seen in behaviour.
